lesson.title: What the Line Assumes About the World
lesson.summary: Valid slope inference rests on a population regression model in which responses at every x vary randomly, and normally, around a true mean line with constant spread, and its LINER conditions are what justify using a t-distribution at all.
lesson.body:
The t-procedure from the previous chapter did not come out of nowhere. It rests on a formal model for how y is generated at every possible value of x, and that model's conditions are exactly what make df equals n minus 2 and the t-distribution the right tools to use.

The population, or process, regression model is usually written as y equals beta0 plus beta1 x plus epsilon. Here beta0 and beta1 are the true, fixed intercept and slope, unknown constants describing the actual linear relationship, and epsilon is a random variable representing the natural scatter of an individual y around the true mean response at that x. The standard assumption is that epsilon follows a Normal distribution centered at 0, with some standard deviation sigma that stays the same at every value of x. Put in words: pick any fixed value of x, and there is an entire distribution of possible y-values there, Normally shaped, centered on the true line beta0 plus beta1 x, spread out by the same amount sigma no matter which x you picked. The sample's least squares line, y-hat equals b0 plus b1 x, is simply our best estimate of that unobservable true line, and each sample residual, y minus y-hat, stands in for an unobservable epsilon.

Checking whether this model is believable comes down to five conditions, sometimes remembered with the acronym LINER.

Linear: the true relationship really is a straight line. Check a scatterplot of the data, and a residual plot, for any leftover curve. A residual plot with no pattern supports linearity, one with a clear curve does not.

Independent: individual observations do not affect each other. If the data were sampled without replacement from a finite population, apply the 10% condition just as in earlier inference procedures.

Normal: at each value of x, the y-values, equivalently the residuals, are approximately Normally distributed. This is usually checked with a histogram or Normal probability plot of the residuals. With very few data points, as in the six-student study hours example, this condition is genuinely hard to check and would normally call for collecting more data before trusting the inference.

Equal variance: the spread of y around the true line stays the same across the whole range of x, sometimes called constant spread or equal standard deviation. A residual plot that fans out or narrows as x increases, a megaphone shape, would violate this condition. A residual plot with roughly even scatter across all x-values supports it.

Random: the data come from a random sample or a randomized experiment, the same foundational requirement behind every inference procedure in this course.

Looking back at the six residuals from the study hours example, approximately negative 0.14, 0.71, negative 1.43, 1.43, negative 0.71, and 0.14, they are small, they sum to zero as residuals always should, and they show no obvious curve or fan shape across the six x-values. That is a mildly reassuring sign, though with only six points it is far too little data to seriously judge Normality or constant spread, a limitation worth stating plainly rather than glossing over.

These conditions are not a formality to check off and forget. They are literally what justifies treating b1 minus beta1, divided by SE(b1), as following a t-distribution with n minus 2 degrees of freedom. If the true scatter around the line were badly skewed, or if it fanned out as x grew, the real sampling distribution of b1 would not match a t-distribution well, and the P-values and confidence intervals from the previous chapter would not be trustworthy, no matter how carefully the arithmetic itself was done.
